title: C.1 Simple Harmonic Motion
subject: IBDP Physics
introduction: Simple harmonic motion describes a type of periodic motion where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and acts in the opposite direction. Many natural and engineered systems show simple harmonic behaviour, including pendulums, springs, vibrations and waves.
learning_objectives: Explain equilibrium position and restoring force.
Analyse displacement, velocity and acceleration relationships.

definitions.meaning: Motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time.
A repeated movement around an equilibrium position.
The position where the resultant force acting on an object is zero.
The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.
The number of oscillations completed per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete oscillation.
A force that acts in the opposite direction to displacement and returns an object towards equilibrium.

core_concepts.heading: Conditions for Simple Harmonic Motion
core_concepts.explanation: For motion to be simple harmonic, the acceleration must be proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position. The further the object moves from equilibrium, the greater the restoring acceleration.

core_concepts.heading: Equilibrium Position
core_concepts.explanation: At equilibrium, the object experiences no resultant force. The velocity is maximum at this point because potential energy has been converted into kinetic energy.

core_concepts.heading: Maximum Displacement
core_concepts.explanation: At maximum displacement, velocity becomes zero and acceleration reaches its maximum value because the restoring force is greatest.

core_concepts.heading: Oscillation Energy
core_concepts.explanation: During oscillation, energy transfers continuously between kinetic energy and potential energy while total mechanical energy remains constant in an ideal system.

formulas.name: Simple Harmonic Motion Acceleration
formulas.explanation: The negative sign shows that acceleration always acts in the opposite direction to displacement, towards the equilibrium position.

formulas.name: Period and Frequency
formulas.explanation: Period and frequency describe how often an oscillation repeats.

formulas.name: Angular Frequency
formulas.explanation: Angular frequency describes the rate of oscillation in radians per second.

formulas.name: Spring Period
formulas.explanation: The period of a spring depends on the mass and stiffness of the spring.

formulas.name: Simple Pendulum Period
formulas.explanation: The period of a pendulum depends on its length and gravitational field strength.

formulas.name: Maximum Velocity
formulas.explanation: Velocity is maximum when the object passes through the equilibrium position.

energy_in_shm.explanation: At maximum displacement, the object stops momentarily before moving back towards equilibrium.
At equilibrium, the object has maximum speed because stored energy has converted into kinetic energy.

graphs.explanation: A displacement-time graph for SHM is sinusoidal. It shows repeated oscillations around the equilibrium position.
important_points: Time between identical points gives the period.

graphs.explanation: Velocity changes continuously during SHM. Maximum velocity occurs at equilibrium.
important_points: Velocity is zero at maximum displacement.

graphs.explanation: Acceleration is opposite to displacement and follows a sinusoidal pattern.
important_points: Maximum acceleration occurs at maximum displacement.

worked_examples.question: A spring system has a mass of 2 kg and spring constant of 50 N/m. Calculate the period.
An oscillator has frequency 5 Hz. Calculate its period.

damping_and_resonance.explanation: Damping is the reduction of amplitude over time due to energy loss from a system. Energy is usually transferred into thermal energy or sound because of resistance.

types.explanation: The system continues oscillating with gradually decreasing amplitude.
The system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillating.
The system returns slowly to equilibrium without oscillating.

damping_and_resonance.explanation: Resonance occurs when an external driving frequency matches the natural frequency of a system. This causes a large increase in amplitude.

applications.explanation: Engineers study vibrations in machines, vehicles and structures to prevent damage caused by unwanted resonance.
Designers analyse natural frequencies to prevent structures from experiencing dangerous vibrations.
Ultrasound systems use wave and vibration principles to create images inside the body.
Pendulums and quartz oscillators use regular periodic motion to measure time accurately.

common_mistakes: Thinking amplitude affects the period of SHM.
Forgetting that acceleration is opposite to displacement.
Assuming velocity is maximum at maximum displacement.
Ignoring energy losses in real systems.
Using degrees instead of radians in angular equations.
ib_exam_tips: Remember that acceleration always points towards equilibrium.
Draw displacement, velocity and acceleration graphs carefully.
Identify maximum and minimum values at important positions.
Use radians when working with angular frequency.
State assumptions when analysing ideal SHM systems.

hl_extension.explanation: The mathematical condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction.
Displacement, velocity and acceleration in SHM have phase differences. Velocity is a quarter cycle ahead of displacement, while acceleration is opposite to displacement.
The total energy of an ideal spring oscillator depends on the spring constant and amplitude.

real_world_applications: Car suspension systems use damping to reduce vibrations.
Seismometers use oscillations to detect earthquakes.
Musical instruments create sound through controlled vibrations.
Aircraft engineers analyse vibrations for safety and comfort.
Robotics systems use motion control based on oscillation principles.

practice_questions.question: Where is the velocity maximum in simple harmonic motion?
Explain why amplitude decreases in a damped oscillator.
practice_questions.answer: Energy is lost from the system due to resistance, reducing the amplitude.

practice_questions.question: Explain what happens when a system experiences resonance.
practice_questions.answer: The amplitude increases greatly when the driving frequency matches the natural frequency.

summary: Simple harmonic motion describes repeated oscillations where the restoring force is proportional to displacement. Understanding SHM helps explain vibrations, waves, engineering systems and natural phenomena. Concepts such as damping, resonance, energy transfer and oscillation equations are essential for analysing periodic motion.
